units.title: Hello, Erlang
units.summary: Write your first Erlang program: a module with a main function that prints text with io:format.

lesson.md: **Erlang** is a language for systems that must run for years without stopping, such as chat servers and phone networks. An Erlang program is made of **modules**, and every module contains **functions**.

lesson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env escript
-module(hello).
-export([main/1]).

main(_) ->
    io:format("Hello, World!~n").

lesson.md: Save this program as `hello.erl` and run it in a terminal with `escript hello.erl`. The tool `escript` comes with Erlang. It reads the file and calls the function `main`. The first line `#!/usr/bin/env escript` marks the file as a script. Every complete program in this course is run this way.

Lines that start with `-` are **attributes**. `-module(hello).` gives the module its name. `-export([main/1]).` makes the function `main` usable from outside the module. `main/1` means: the function `main` with **one** argument. This number is called the **arity**.

`main(_) ->` starts the function. `escript` passes the command-line arguments as the one argument; the `_` means that you ignore it. After the arrow `->` comes the body. The period `.` ends the function, and every attribute ends with a period too.

`io:format(...)` calls the function `format` from the module `io`. The colon `:` separates the module name from the function name. The text goes in double quotes. `~n` inside the text starts a new line.

lesson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env escript
-module(lines).
-export([main/1]).

main(_) ->
    io:format("Line 1~n"),
    io:format("Line 2~n").

lesson.md: A body can have several **expressions**. A comma `,` separates them, and they run from top to bottom. Only the last one ends with the period.

To print values, write `~p` in the text and give the values as a second argument: a **list** in square brackets `[...]`. Each `~p` is replaced by the next value from the list. Erlang calculates `2 + 3` before it prints.

lesson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env escript
-module(sum).
-export([main/1]).

main(_) ->
    io:format("~p + ~p = ~p~n", [2, 3, 2 + 3]).

lesson.md: Without `~n` the next output continues on the same line. `io:format("a")` followed by `io:format("b~n")` prints `ab`.
Watch the punctuation: a period in the middle of a body ends the function too early, and the next line is then an error. Between expressions you need a comma.

units.title: Values and types
units.summary: Calculate with integers and floats, and get to know atoms, booleans, strings and binaries.

lesson.md: Erlang calculates with `+`, `-` and `*`. The operator `/` always gives a **float** (a decimal number), even when the result is whole. For whole numbers, `div` divides without the rest and `rem` gives the rest.

lesson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env escript
-module(calc).
-export([main/1]).

main(_) ->
    io:format("~p ~p ~p ~p~n", [7 + 2, 7 * 2, 7 div 2, 7 rem 2]),
    io:format("~p~n", [7 / 2]),
    io:format("~p~n", [6 / 2]).

lesson.md: A float needs a digit on both sides of the point: write `0.5`, not `.5`. `round` rounds a float to the nearest integer, and `trunc` cuts off the decimals. Integers have no size limit, so you can calculate with very big numbers.

lesson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env escript
-module(floats).
-export([main/1]).

main(_) ->
    io:format("~p~n", [2.5 * 2]),
    io:format("~p ~p~n", [round(2.7), trunc(2.7)]),
    io:format("~p~n", [12345678901234567890 * 10]).

lesson.md: An **atom** is a constant whose value is its own name, such as `ok`, `error` or `red`. Atoms start with a lowercase letter. Words that start with an uppercase letter are variables; you meet them in the next unit.

lesson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env escript
-module(atoms).
-export([main/1]).

main(_) ->
    io:format("~p ~p~n", [ok, red]),
    io:format("~p~n", [ok == ok]),
    io:format("~p~n", [ok == error]).

lesson.md: The booleans are the atoms `true` and `false`. You compare with `==`, `/=` (not equal), `<`, `>`, `>=` and `=<` (careful: not `<=`). `==` treats `1` and `1.0` as equal; `=:=` also compares the type. `and`, `or` and `not` combine booleans.

lesson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env escript
-module(compare).
-export([main/1]).

main(_) ->
    io:format("~p ~p~n", [3 =< 4, 5 /= 5]),
    io:format("~p ~p~n", [1 == 1.0, 1 =:= 1.0]),
    io:format("~p~n", [not (true and false)]).

lesson.md: A string in double quotes like `"Hello"` is a **list of character codes**. `~s` prints it as text. `++` joins two lists, and `length` counts the elements. Because `~p` shows a list of character codes as text, `[72, 105]` prints as `"Hi"`.

lesson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env escript
-module(strings).
-export([main/1]).

main(_) ->
    io:format("~s~n", ["Hello" ++ " World"]),
    io:format("~p~n", [length("Hello")]),
    io:format("~p~n", ["abc" == [97, 98, 99]]),
    io:format("~p~n", [[72, 105]]).

lesson.md: A **binary** like `<<"Erlang">>` stores text as compact bytes. Modern Erlang code uses binaries for text a lot. `~s` prints binaries as text too, and `byte_size` counts the bytes.

lesson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env escript
-module(binaries).
-export([main/1]).

main(_) ->
    io:format("~s~n", [<<"Erlang">>]),
    io:format("~p~n", [<<"Erlang">>]),
    io:format("~p~n", [byte_size(<<"Erlang">>)]).

card: `"hi"` is a list, `<<"hi">>` is a binary

units.title: Variables and pattern matching
units.summary: Bind values to variables once, and use pattern matching to take tuples and lists apart.

lesson.md: A **variable** starts with an uppercase letter, for example `Name` or `Age`. The `=` gives it a value. We say the variable is **bound** to the value.

lesson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env escript
-module(vars).
-export([main/1]).

main(_) ->
    Name = "Ada",
    Age = 36,
    io:format("~s is ~p~n", [Name, Age]).

lesson.md: A variable is bound only **once** and never changes. This is called **single assignment**. When you need a new value, you use a new name.

lesson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env escript
-module(single).
-export([main/1]).

main(_) ->
    Count = 5,
    Count2 = Count + 1,
    io:format("~p ~p~n", [Count, Count2]).

lesson.md: `Count = Count + 1` does not add one. `Count` is already `5`, so Erlang checks `5 = 6`, which fails. The program stops with a `badmatch` error.

This is because `=` is the **match operator**. The left side is a **pattern**. If it contains a variable without a value, the variable gets bound. If the variable already has a value, both sides must be equal. So `10 = X` works when `X` is `10`.

A **tuple** groups a fixed number of values in curly braces, for example `{point, 3, 4}`. The first element is often an atom that says what the tuple is. `element(2, T)` returns the second element, and `tuple_size(T)` the number of elements.

lesson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env escript
-module(tuples).
-export([main/1]).

main(_) ->
    Point = {point, 3, 4},
    io:format("~p~n", [Point]),
    io:format("~p ~p~n", [element(2, Point), tuple_size(Point)]).

lesson.md: Pattern matching takes a tuple apart. The pattern `{point, X, Y}` matches any tuple with three elements whose first element is the atom `point`. `X` and `Y` get bound to the other two values.

lesson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env escript
-module(unpack).
-export([main/1]).

main(_) ->
    Point = {point, 3, 4},
    {point, X, Y} = Point,
    io:format("X = ~p, Y = ~p~n", [X, Y]).

lesson.md: The underscore `_` matches any value and ignores it. Names that start with an underscore, such as `_Year`, also match anything; use them when you want to show what the value means. Lists in square brackets can be matched in the same way.

lesson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env escript
-module(results).
-export([main/1]).

main(_) ->
    {ok, Result} = {ok, 42},
    [A, B, _] = [10, 20, 30],
    io:format("~p ~p ~p~n", [Result, A, B]).

lesson.md: Many Erlang functions return `{ok, Value}` when they succeed and `{error, Reason}` when they fail. With a pattern like `{ok, Value}` you take the result out and check for success in one step.

card: `{point, X, Y} = P` takes a tuple apart

units.title: Functions
units.summary: Write your own functions with several clauses and guards, and store anonymous functions in variables.

lesson.md: You write a function as `name(Arguments) -> Body.` and call it with `name(Values)`. A module can have many functions. `main` can call the other functions of the module directly; only functions called from outside need `-export`.

lesson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env escript
-module(double).
-export([main/1]).

main(_) ->
    io:format("~p~n", [double(21)]).

double(X) ->
    X * 2.

lesson.md: Erlang has no `return` keyword. A function returns the value of its **last expression**. A function with two arguments has the arity 2, so the function below is `area/2`.

lesson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env escript
-module(area).
-export([main/1]).

main(_) ->
    io:format("~p~n", [area(3, 4)]).

area(Width, Height) ->
    Width * Height.

lesson.md: A function can have several **clauses**. Each clause has its own pattern for the arguments, and a semicolon `;` separates the clauses. Erlang tries them from top to bottom and runs the first one that matches. The last clause ends with a period.
Functions with the same name but a different arity are different functions. `greet/1` and `greet/2` can both exist in one module.

A **guard** adds a condition to a clause. It starts with `when` after the arguments. The clause runs only when the pattern matches **and** the guard is `true`. Guards can use comparisons and tests like `is_integer(X)`.
If no clause matches, the program stops with a `function_clause` error. Order the clauses from the most specific to the most general.
An **anonymous function** has no name: `fun(X) -> X * 3 end`. You can store it in a variable and call it like a function. You can also pass it to another function as an argument.

lesson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env escript
-module(funs).
-export([main/1]).

main(_) ->
    Triple = fun(X) -> X * 3 end,
    io:format("~p~n", [Triple(5)]),
    Apply = fun(F, V) -> F(V) end,
    io:format("~p~n", [Apply(Triple, 2)]).

card: The last expression is the return value

units.title: Lists
units.summary: Take lists apart with [H | T], use lists:map, lists:filter and lists:sum, and write list comprehensions.

lesson.md: A **list** holds any number of values: `[10, 20, 30]`. `length` counts the elements, `hd` returns the first element (the **head**), and `tl` returns the rest (the **tail**). `++` joins two lists.

lesson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env escript
-module(nums).
-export([main/1]).

main(_) ->
    Nums = [10, 20, 30],
    io:format("~p ~p~n", [length(Nums), hd(Nums)]),
    io:format("~p~n", [tl(Nums)]),
    io:format("~p~n", [Nums ++ [40]]).

lesson.md: The pattern `[H | T]` splits a list into its head and its tail. The bar `|` separates the first element from the rest. You can also use `|` to build a list: `[0 | Nums]` puts `0` in front of `Nums`.

lesson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env escript
-module(headtail).
-export([main/1]).

main(_) ->
    [First | Rest] = [a, b, c],
    io:format("~p ~p~n", [First, Rest]),
    io:format("~p~n", [[z | Rest]]).

lesson.md: The empty list `[]` has no head, so `[H | T] = []` fails. A list with one element has the empty list as its tail: `[x]` is the same as `[x | []]`.

The module `lists` has many useful functions. `lists:sum` adds all numbers, `lists:max` finds the biggest, `lists:sort` sorts, `lists:reverse` reverses, and `lists:member` checks if a value is in the list.

lesson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env escript
-module(listsmod).
-export([main/1]).

main(_) ->
    Nums = [3, 1, 2],
    io:format("~p ~p~n", [lists:sum(Nums), lists:max(Nums)]),
    io:format("~p ~p~n", [lists:sort(Nums), lists:reverse(Nums)]),
    io:format("~p~n", [lists:member(2, Nums)]).

lesson.md: `lists:map(F, List)` calls the function `F` for every element and returns a list of the results. `lists:filter(F, List)` keeps only the elements for which `F` returns `true`. The function comes first, the list second.

lesson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env escript
-module(mapfilter).
-export([main/1]).

main(_) ->
    Nums = [1, 2, 3, 4],
    Doubled = lists:map(fun(X) -> X * 2 end, Nums),
    Even = lists:filter(fun(X) -> X rem 2 == 0 end, Nums),
    io:format("~p ~p~n", [Doubled, Even]).

lesson.md: A **list comprehension** builds a new list in one line: `[X * X || X <- Nums]`. Read it as: the list of `X * X` for every `X` taken from `Nums`. The arrow `<-` takes the elements one by one. Conditions after a comma keep only some elements.

lesson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env escript
-module(comp).
-export([main/1]).

main(_) ->
    Nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5],
    io:format("~p~n", [[X * X || X <- Nums]]),
    io:format("~p~n", [[X || X <- Nums, X > 2]]).

card: `[X * 2 || X <- L, X > 0]` is a list comprehension

units.title: Recursion
units.summary: Repeat work with functions that call themselves, and use accumulators for tail recursion.

lesson.md: Erlang has no `for` or `while` loops. To repeat something, a function calls itself. This is called **recursion**.

lesson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env escript
-module(countdown).
-export([main/1]).

main(_) ->
    countdown(3).

countdown(0) ->
    io:format("Go!~n");
countdown(N) ->
    io:format("~p~n", [N]),
    countdown(N - 1).

lesson.md: Every recursive function needs a **base case**: a clause that stops. Here it is `countdown(0)`. The other clause makes the problem smaller (`N - 1`) and calls the function again.
Lists fit recursion well. The base case is the empty list `[]`. The other clause takes the list apart with `[H | T]` and calls itself with the tail.

lesson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env escript
-module(sum).
-export([main/1]).

main(_) ->
    io:format("~p~n", [sum([1, 2, 3, 4])]).

sum([]) -> 0;
sum([H | T]) -> H + sum(T).

lesson.md: Step by step: `sum([1, 2, 3])` is `1 + sum([2, 3])`, which is `1 + 2 + sum([3])`, which is `1 + 2 + 3 + sum([])`, and `sum([])` is `0`. Each call must wait for the next one, so a long list needs a lot of memory.
An **accumulator** is an extra argument that carries the result so far. `sum/1` starts the work by calling `sum/2` with `0`. Remember: `sum/1` and `sum/2` are different functions.

lesson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env escript
-module(acc).
-export([main/1]).

main(_) ->
    io:format("~p~n", [sum([1, 2, 3, 4])]).

sum(List) -> sum(List, 0).

sum([], Acc) -> Acc;
sum([H | T], Acc) -> sum(T, Acc + H).

lesson.md: In `sum(T, Acc + H)` the recursive call is the **last** thing the function does. This is a **tail call**, and the function is **tail recursive**. Erlang does not need extra memory for tail calls. In `H + sum(T)` the addition comes after the call, so it is not a tail call.

lesson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env escript
-module(fact).
-export([main/1]).

main(_) ->
    io:format("~p~n", [fact(5)]),
    io:format("~p~n", [fact(20)]).

fact(N) -> fact(N, 1).

fact(0, Acc) -> Acc;
fact(N, Acc) when N > 0 -> fact(N - 1, Acc * N).

lesson.md: When you build a list with an accumulator, each new element goes to the front with `[New | Acc]`. The result is then in reverse order, so the base case calls `lists:reverse`.

lesson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env escript
-module(double).
-export([main/1]).

main(_) ->
    io:format("~p~n", [double_all([1, 2, 3])]).

double_all(List) -> double_all(List, []).

double_all([], Acc) -> lists:reverse(Acc);
double_all([H | T], Acc) -> double_all(T, [H * 2 | Acc]).

lesson.md: A recursion that never reaches its base case never stops. For example, `countdown(-1)` above never reaches `0`. A guard like `when N > 0` protects against this.

card: Accumulator: `sum([H | T], Acc) -> sum(T, Acc + H).`
Tail call: the recursive call is the last step

exercises.prompt: What does `count([a, b, c])` return?
exercises.explain: Each clause with `[_ | T]` adds 1 for one element. The empty list adds 0.

Which clause is the base case?
exercises.explain: The base case stops the recursion: it does not call `len` again.
After the call `sum(T)` returns, the function still adds `H`. So the call is not the last step.

exercises.explain: The new element must go in front of the accumulator. Write `rev(T, [H | Acc])`.

exercises.explain: The clause takes one element off the list, counts it with `1` and adds the length of the tail.

units.title: Maps and tuples
units.summary: Store key-value pairs in maps, read and update them, and use tagged tuples as small records.

lesson.md: A **map** stores pairs of keys and values: `#{name => "Ada", age => 36}`. The arrow `=>` links a key to its value. Keys are often atoms. `maps:get(Key, Map)` returns the value, and `map_size` counts the pairs.

lesson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env escript
-module(user).
-export([main/1]).

main(_) ->
    User = #{name => "Ada", age => 36},
    io:format("~s~n", [maps:get(name, User)]),
    io:format("~p~n", [maps:get(age, User)]),
    io:format("~p~n", [map_size(User)]).

lesson.md: If a key is missing, `maps:get(Key, Map)` stops the program with a `badkey` error. `maps:get(Key, Map, Default)` returns the default value instead. `maps:is_key` checks if a key exists.

lesson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env escript
-module(stock).
-export([main/1]).

main(_) ->
    Stock = #{apple => 3},
    io:format("~p~n", [maps:get(pear, Stock, 0)]),
    io:format("~p~n", [maps:is_key(apple, Stock)]).

lesson.md: Maps never change, like variables. `maps:put(Key, Value, Map)` returns a **new** map with the pair added or replaced. The short form `Map#{Key => Value}` does the same. The old map stays as it was.

lesson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env escript
-module(prices).
-export([main/1]).

main(_) ->
    Prices = #{tea => 2},
    Prices2 = maps:put(coffee, 3, Prices),
    Prices3 = Prices2#{tea => 5},
    io:format("~p ~p~n", [map_size(Prices), map_size(Prices2)]),
    io:format("~p~n", [maps:get(tea, Prices3)]).

lesson.md: You can take values out of a map with pattern matching. In a pattern you write `:=` instead of `=>`. The pattern matches when the map has these keys; other keys are ignored.

lesson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env escript
-module(person).
-export([main/1]).

main(_) ->
    User = #{name => "Bo", age => 25, city => "Oslo"},
    #{name := Name, city := City} = User,
    io:format("~s lives in ~s~n", [Name, City]).

lesson.md: `maps:to_list` returns all pairs as `{Key, Value}` tuples, and `maps:keys` returns the keys. The order is not fixed, so sort the result with `lists:sort` when the order matters.

lesson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env escript
-module(ages).
-export([main/1]).

main(_) ->
    Ages = #{bo => 25, ada => 36},
    io:format("~p~n", [lists:sort(maps:to_list(Ages))]),
    io:format("~p~n", [lists:sort(maps:keys(Ages))]).

lesson.md: A tuple with an atom as its first element works like a small record: `{book, Title, Year}`. The atom is a **tag** that says what the data is. Functions can have one clause for each tag. Use a tuple for a few fixed fields and a map when you want named keys.

lesson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env escript
-module(records).
-export([main/1]).

main(_) ->
    Book = {book, "Dune", 1965},
    io:format("~s~n", [describe(Book)]),
    io:format("~s~n", [describe({film, "Up"})]).

describe({book, Title, _Year}) -> "Book: " ++ Title;
describe({film, Title}) -> "Film: " ++ Title.

card: `M#{b => 2}` or `maps:put(b, 2, M)` gives a new map
`#{a := A} = M` takes a value out
`{book, Title, Year}` is a tagged tuple

units.title: Processes
units.summary: Start processes with spawn, send them messages with !, and wait for answers with receive.

lesson.md: An Erlang program can run thousands of small **processes** at the same time. Each process has its own memory. Processes do not share variables; they work together by sending **messages**.

`spawn(Fun)` starts a new process that runs the function `Fun`, and returns its **process identifier**, or **pid**. `self()` returns the pid of the process that is running the code. `is_pid` checks if a value is a pid.

lesson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env escript
-module(start).
-export([main/1]).

main(_) ->
    Pid = spawn(fun() -> ok end),
    io:format("~p~n", [is_pid(Pid)]),
    io:format("~p~n", [is_pid(self())]).

lesson.md: `Pid ! Message` sends a message to a process. A message can be any value. It goes into the **mailbox** of the receiving process. The sender does not wait.
`receive` waits for a message and matches it against patterns, like the clauses of a function. The block ends with `end`. A process can also send a message to itself.

lesson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env escript
-module(mailbox).
-export([main/1]).

main(_) ->
    self() ! hello,
    receive
        hello -> io:format("Got hello~n")
    end.

lesson.md: To get an answer, send your own pid with the message, for example `{self(), 21}`. The other process uses this pid to reply. Here the new process doubles the number and sends back `{result, 42}`.

lesson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env escript
-module(reply).
-export([main/1]).

main(_) ->
    Doubler = spawn(fun() ->
        receive
            {From, N} -> From ! {result, N * 2}
        end
    end),
    Doubler ! {self(), 21},
    receive
        {result, R} -> io:format("Result: ~p~n", [R])
    end.

lesson.md: A process that serves many messages runs a recursive **loop**. The argument of the loop is the state of the process. After each message, the loop calls itself with the new state. The atom `stop` ends the loop.

lesson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env escript
-module(counter).
-export([main/1]).

main(_) ->
    Counter = spawn(fun() -> loop(0) end),
    Counter ! add,
    Counter ! add,
    Counter ! add,
    Counter ! {get, self()},
    receive
        {count, N} -> io:format("Count: ~p~n", [N])
    end,
    Counter ! stop.

loop(N) ->
    receive
        add ->
            loop(N + 1);
        {get, From} ->
            From ! {count, N},
            loop(N);
        stop ->
            ok
    end.

lesson.md: Messages from one process to another arrive in the order they were sent. Messages from different processes can arrive in any order. That is why the examples wait for a reply before they print.
`receive` can wait forever. With `after` you set a time limit in milliseconds. If no matching message arrives in time, the code after `after` runs.

lesson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env escript
-module(timeout).
-export([main/1]).

main(_) ->
    receive
        hello -> io:format("Got hello~n")
    after 100 ->
        io:format("No message~n")
    end.

lesson.md: `receive` takes only messages that match one of its patterns. Other messages stay in the mailbox. If no message ever matches and there is no `after`, the process waits forever.

card: `receive Pattern -> ... end` waits for a message
`self()` is the pid of the current process

exercises.explain: Sending never waits. The message goes into the mailbox, and the sender continues at once.
